177	1. **Find the design system**: Search for design system documentation, component libraries, style guides, or token definitions. Study the core patterns: design principles, target audience, color tokens, spacing scale, typography styles, component API, motion conventions.
178	2. **Note the conventions**: How are shared components imported? What spacing scale is used? Which colors come from tokens vs hard-coded values? What motion and interaction patterns are established? What flow shapes are used for comparable actions (modal vs full-page, inline vs route, save-on-blur vs explicit submit)?
179	3. **Identify drift, then name the root cause**: For every deviation, classify it as a **missing token** (the value should exist in the system but doesn't), a **one-off implementation** (a shared component already exists but wasn't used), or a **conceptual misalignment** (the feature's flow, IA, or hierarchy doesn't match neighboring features). The fix differs by category: patch the value, swap to the shared component, or rework the flow. Fixing the symptom without naming the cause is how drift compounds.
180	
181	If a design system exists, polish **must** align the feature with it. If none exists, polish against the conventions visible in the codebase. **If anything about the system is ambiguous, ask. Never guess at design system principles.**
182	
183	## Pre-Polish Assessment
184	
185	Understand the current state and goals before touching anything:
186	
187	1. **Review completeness**:
188	   - Is it functionally complete?
189	   - Are there known issues to preserve (mark with TODOs)?
190	   - What's the quality bar? (MVP vs flagship feature?)
191	   - When does it ship? (How much time for polish?)
192	
193	2. **Think experience-first**: Who actually uses this, and what's the best possible experience for them? Effective design beats decorative polish; a feature that looks beautiful but fights the user's flow is not polished. Walk the path from their perspective before opening DevTools.
194	
195	3. **Identify polish areas**:
196	   - Visual inconsistencies
197	   - Spacing and alignment issues
198	   - Interaction state gaps
199	   - Copy inconsistencies
200	   - Edge cases and error states
201	   - Loading and transition smoothness
202	   - Information architecture and flow drift (does this feature reveal complexity the way neighboring features do?)
203	
204	4. **Pull in any prior critique** (optional signal): If `/impeccable critique` has been run on the same target, its priority issues are a useful prior for what to address first. Resolve the target to a file path or URL, then:
205	   ```bash
206	   slug=$(node .pi/skills/impeccable/scripts/critique-storage.mjs slug "<resolved>")
207	   node .pi/skills/impeccable/scripts/critique-storage.mjs latest "$slug"
208	   ```
209	   Exit 0 with body = found; fold the P0/P1 items into your polish list and mention the snapshot path so the user sees what you read. Exit 2 = no snapshot, continue without it. The critique is one input among many. Do your own pass either way.
210	
211	5. **Triage cosmetic vs functional**: Classify each issue as **cosmetic** (looks off, doesn't impede the user) or **functional** (breaks, blocks, or confuses the experience). When polish time is tight, functional issues ship first; cosmetic ones can land in a follow-up. Quality should be consistent; never perfect one corner while leaving another rough.
212	
213	**CRITICAL**: Polish is the last step, not the first. Don't polish work that's not functionally complete.
214	
215	## Polish Systematically
216	
217	Work through these dimensions methodically:
218	
219	### Visual Alignment & Spacing
220	
221	- **Pixel-perfect alignment**: Everything lines up to grid
222	- **Consistent spacing**: All gaps use spacing scale (no random 13px gaps)
223	- **Optical alignment**: Adjust for visual weight (icons may need offset for optical centering)
224	- **Responsive consistency**: Spacing and alignment work at all breakpoints
225	- **Grid adherence**: Elements snap to baseline grid
226	
227	**Check**:
228	- Enable grid overlay and verify alignment
229	- Check spacing with browser inspector
230	- Test at multiple viewport sizes
231	- Look for elements that "feel" off
232	
233	### Information Architecture & Flow
234	
235	Visual polish on a misshapen flow is wasted work. Match the *shape* of the experience to the system, not just the surface.
236	
237	- **Progressive disclosure**: Match how much is revealed when, compared to neighboring features. A settings page exposing 40 fields when the rest of the app reveals 5 at a time is drift, even if every field is perfectly styled.
238	- **Established user flows**: Multi-step actions follow the same shape as comparable flows elsewhere: modal vs full-page, inline edit vs separate route, save-on-blur vs explicit submit, optimistic vs pessimistic updates.
239	- **Hierarchy & complexity**: The same conceptual weight gets the same visual weight throughout. Primary actions don't become tertiary in one corner of the product, and tertiary actions don't shout.
240	- **Empty, loading, and arrival transitions**: How content arrives, updates, and leaves matches how it does in adjacent features.
241	- **Naming and mental model**: The feature uses the same nouns and verbs as the rest of the system. A "Workspace" here shouldn't be a "Project" three screens away.
242	
243	### Typography Refinement
244	
245	- **Hierarchy consistency**: Same elements use same sizes/weights throughout
246	- **Line length**: 45-75 characters for body text
247	- **Line height**: Appropriate for font size and context
248	- **Widows & orphans**: No single words on last line
249	- **Hyphenation**: Appropriate for language and column width
250	- **Kerning**: Adjust letter spacing where needed (especially headlines)
251	- **Font loading**: No FOUT/FOIT flashes
252	
253	### Color & Contrast
254	
255	- **Contrast ratios**: All text meets WCAG standards
256	- **Consistent token usage**: No hard-coded colors, all use design tokens
257	- **Theme consistency**: Works in all theme variants
258	- **Color meaning**: Same colors mean same things throughout
259	- **Accessible focus**: Focus indicators visible with sufficient contrast
260	- **Gray on color**: Never put gray text on colored backgrounds; use a shade of that color or transparency
261	
262	### Interaction States
263	
264	Every interactive element needs all states:
265	
266	- **Default**: Resting state
267	- **Hover**: Subtle feedback (color, scale, shadow)
268	- **Focus**: Keyboard focus indicator (never remove without replacement)
269	- **Active**: Click/tap feedback
270	- **Disabled**: Clearly non-interactive
271	- **Loading**: Async action feedback
272	- **Error**: Validation or error state
273	- **Success**: Successful completion
274	
275	**Missing states create confusion and broken experiences**.
276	
277	### Micro-interactions & Transitions
278	
279	- **Smooth transitions**: All state changes animated appropriately (150-300ms)
280	- **Consistent easing**: Use ease-out-quart/quint/expo for natural deceleration. Never bounce or elastic; they feel dated.
281	- **No jank**: Smooth animations; use atmospheric blur/filter/mask/shadow effects when they add polish, but bound expensive paint areas and avoid casual layout-property animation
282	- **Appropriate motion**: Motion serves purpose, not decoration
283	- **Reduced motion**: Respects `prefers-reduced-motion`
284	
285	### Content & Copy
286	
287	- **Consistent terminology**: Same things called same names throughout
288	- **Consistent capitalization**: Title Case vs Sentence case applied consistently
289	- **Grammar & spelling**: No typos
290	- **Appropriate length**: Not too wordy, not too terse
291	- **Punctuation consistency**: Periods on sentences, not on labels (unless all labels have them)
292	
293	### Icons & Images
294	
295	- **Consistent style**: All icons from same family or matching style
296	- **Appropriate sizing**: Icons sized consistently for context
297	- **Proper alignment**: Icons align with adjacent text optically
298	- **Alt text**: All images have descriptive alt text
299	- **Loading states**: Images don't cause layout shift, proper aspect ratios
300	- **Retina support**: 2x assets for high-DPI screens
301	
302	### Forms & Inputs
303	
304	- **Label consistency**: All inputs properly labeled
305	- **Required indicators**: Clear and consistent
306	- **Error messages**: Helpful and consistent
307	- **Tab order**: Logical keyboard navigation
308	- **Auto-focus**: Appropriate (don't overuse)
309	- **Validation timing**: Consistent (on blur vs on submit)
310	
311	### Edge Cases & Error States
312	
313	- **Loading states**: All async actions have loading feedback
314	- **Empty states**: Helpful empty states, not just blank space
315	- **Error states**: Clear error messages with recovery paths
316	- **Success states**: Confirmation of successful actions
317	- **Long content**: Handles very long names, descriptions, etc.
318	- **No content**: Handles missing data gracefully
319	- **Offline**: Appropriate offline handling (if applicable)
320	
321	### Responsiveness
322	
323	- **All breakpoints**: Test mobile, tablet, desktop
324	- **Touch targets**: 44x44px minimum on touch devices
325	- **Readable text**: No text smaller than 14px on mobile
326	- **No horizontal scroll**: Content fits viewport
327	- **Appropriate reflow**: Content adapts logically
328	
329	### Performance
330	
331	- **Fast initial load**: Optimize critical path
332	- **No layout shift**: Elements don't jump after load (CLS)
333	- **Smooth interactions**: No lag or jank
334	- **Optimized images**: Appropriate formats and sizes
335	- **Lazy loading**: Off-screen content loads lazily
336	
337	### Code Quality
338	
339	- **Remove console logs**: No debug logging in production
340	- **Remove commented code**: Clean up dead code
341	- **Remove unused imports**: Clean up unused dependencies
342	- **Consistent naming**: Variables and functions follow conventions
343	- **Type safety**: No TypeScript `any` or ignored errors
344	- **Accessibility**: Proper ARIA labels and semantic HTML
345	
346	## Polish Checklist
347	
348	Go through systematically:
349	
350	- [ ] Aligned to the design system (drift named and resolved by root cause)
351	- [ ] Information architecture and flow shape match neighboring features
352	- [ ] Visual alignment perfect at all breakpoints
353	- [ ] Spacing uses design tokens consistently
354	- [ ] Typography hierarchy consistent
355	- [ ] All interactive states implemented
356	- [ ] All transitions smooth (60fps)
357	- [ ] Copy is consistent and polished
358	- [ ] Icons are consistent and properly sized
359	- [ ] All forms properly labeled and validated
360	- [ ] Error states are helpful
361	- [ ] Loading states are clear
362	- [ ] Empty states are welcoming
363	- [ ] Touch targets are 44x44px minimum
364	- [ ] Contrast ratios meet WCAG AA
365	- [ ] Keyboard navigation works
366	- [ ] Focus indicators visible
367	- [ ] No console errors or warnings
368	- [ ] No layout shift on load
369	- [ ] Works in all supported browsers
370	- [ ] Respects reduced motion preference
371	- [ ] Code is clean (no TODOs, console.logs, commented code)
372	
373	**IMPORTANT**: Polish is about details. Zoom in. Squint at it. Use it yourself. The little things add up.
374	
375	Sweat the details. Zoom in until the alignment is right and the spacing reads as deliberate. Then ship.
376	
377	**NEVER**:
378	- Polish before it's functionally complete
379	- Polish without aligning to the design system; that's decoration on drift
380	- Guess at design system principles instead of asking when something is ambiguous
381	- Spend hours on polish if it ships in 30 minutes (triage)
382	- Introduce bugs while polishing (test thoroughly)
383	- Ignore systematic issues (if spacing is off everywhere, fix the system, not just one screen)
384	- Perfect one thing while leaving others rough (consistent quality level)
385	- Create new one-off components when design system equivalents exist
386	- Hard-code values that should use design tokens
387	- Introduce new patterns or flows that diverge from established ones
388	
389	## Final Verification
390	
391	Before marking as done:
392	
393	- **Use it yourself**: Actually interact with the feature.
394	- **Test on real devices**: Not just browser DevTools.
395	- **Ask someone else to review**: Fresh eyes catch things.
396	- **Compare to design**: Match intended design.
397	- **Check all states**: Don't just test happy path.
398	- **Treat automation carefully**: Run detector or QA commands when they are available and relevant, fix their defects, but never cite a clean result as proof that the work is polished.
399	
400	## Clean Up
401	
402	After polishing, ensure code quality:
403	
404	- **Replace custom implementations**: If the design system provides a component you reimplemented, switch to the shared version.
405	- **Remove orphaned code**: Delete unused styles, components, or files made obsolete by polish.
406	- **Consolidate tokens**: If you introduced new values, check whether they should be tokens.
407	- **Verify DRYness**: Look for duplication introduced during polishing and consolidate.
408	# Product register
409	
410	When design SERVES the product: app UIs, admin dashboards, settings panels, data tables, tools, authenticated surfaces, anything where the user is in a task.
411	
412	## The product slop test
413	
414	Not "would someone say AI made this." Familiarity is often a feature here. The test is: would a user fluent in the category's best tools (Linear, Figma, Notion, Raycast, Stripe come to mind) sit down and trust this interface, or pause at every subtly-off component?
415	
416	Product UI's failure mode isn't flatness, it's strangeness without purpose: over-decorated buttons, mismatched form controls, gratuitous motion, display fonts where labels should be, invented affordances for standard tasks. The bar is earned familiarity. The tool should disappear into the task.
417	
418	## Typography
419	
420	- **One family is often right.** Product UIs don't need display/body pairing. A well-tuned sans carries headings, buttons, labels, body, data.
421	- **Fixed rem scale, not fluid.** Clamp-sized headings don't serve product UI. Users view at consistent DPI, and a fluid h1 that shrinks in a sidebar looks worse, not better.
422	- **Tighter scale ratio.** 1.125–1.2 between steps is typical. More type elements here than on brand surfaces; exaggerated contrast creates noise.
423	- **Line length still applies for prose** (65–75ch). Data and compact UI can run denser; tables at 120ch+ are fine.
424	
425	## Color
426	
427	Product defaults to Restrained. A single surface can earn Committed (a dashboard where one category color carries a report, an onboarding flow with a drenched welcome screen), but Restrained is the floor.
428	
429	- State-rich semantic vocabulary: hover, focus, active, disabled, selected, loading, error, warning, success, info. Standardize these.
430	- Accent color used for primary actions, current selection, and state indicators only, not decoration.
431	- A second neutral layer for sidebars, toolbars, and panels (slightly cooler or warmer than the content surface).
432	
433	## Layout
434	
435	- Responsive behavior is structural (collapse sidebar, responsive table, breakpoint-driven columns), not fluid typography.
436	
437	## Components
438	
439	Every interactive component has: default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error. Don't ship with half of these.
440	
441	- Skeleton states for loading, not spinners in the middle of content.
442	- Empty states that teach the interface, not "nothing here."
443	- Consistent affordances across the surface. Same button shape. Same form-control vocabulary. Same icon style.
444	
445	## Motion
446	
447	- 150–250 ms on most transitions. Users are in flow; don't make them wait for choreography.
448	- Motion conveys state, not decoration. State change, feedback, loading, reveal: nothing else.
449	- No orchestrated page-load sequences. Product loads into a task; users don't want to watch it load.
450	
451	## Product bans (on top of the shared absolute bans)
452	
453	- Decorative motion that doesn't convey state.
454	- Inconsistent component vocabulary across screens. If the "save" button looks different in two places, one is wrong.
455	- Display fonts in UI labels, buttons, data.
456	- Reinventing standard affordances for flavor (custom scrollbars, weird form controls, non-standard modals).
457	- Heavy color or full-saturation accents on inactive states.
458	- Modal as first thought. Modals are usually laziness. Exhaust inline / progressive alternatives first.
459	
460	## Product permissions
461	
462	Product can afford things brand surfaces can't.
463	
464	- System fonts and familiar sans defaults (Inter, SF Pro, system-ui stacks).
465	- Standard navigation patterns: top bar + side nav, breadcrumbs, tabs, command palettes.
466	- Density. Tables with many rows, panels with many labels, dense information when users need it.
467	- Consistency over surprise. The same visual vocabulary screen to screen is a virtue; delight is saved for moments, not pages.

7	## Users
8	
9	Initially a single person: the author, dogfooding a single-account desktop client (macOS first) against their own Gmail inbox in focused, keyboard-first sessions. They move through a high volume of mail quickly, want to reach "done" on each conversation, and need to trust that every action (archive, bulk processing, undo, send) did exactly what it claimed. The provider's own client remains the fallback.
10	
11	Longer term: technically capable people who want to compose their own email workflow (custom views, triage signals, commands, automations), manually or with an agent, without rebuilding sync, credentials, or send safety.
12	
13	The primary task on most screens is triage: scan the list, open a conversation, decide, act, move on.
14	
15	## Product Purpose
16	
17	A composable email client: a trusted mail engine (sync, safe rendering, credentials, action execution) with replaceable signals, views, commands, and workflows on top. It ships an opinionated reference experience, a compact Superhuman-style browsing and keyboard flow, rather than a blank toolkit.
18	
19	The near-term goal is a complete, trustworthy inbox-processing session. Strategic scope is set by `docs/adr/0001-single-account-desktop-email-client.md` and `superhuman-email-browsing-ux-spec.md`; this file does not expand it.
20	
21	Success looks like: the author processes their inbox faster and with more confidence than in their previous client, and every automated or bulk action is previewable, reported honestly (including partial success and "outcome unknown"), and undoable where undo is real.
22	
23	## Brand Personality
24	
25	**Focused, precise, trustworthy.**
26	
27	- **Focused:** the interface recedes so the mail and the next decision are what's on screen. Dense, quiet, few competing elements.
28	- **Precise:** exact states, exact counts, exact wording. No vague "something went wrong", no rounded-off truth about what happened.
29	- **Trustworthy:** the client never overstates what it did. Pending, failed, partial, and ambiguous outcomes are visible and distinct. Automation shows its work before it acts.
30	
31	Voice is terse and factual: short labels, plain verbs, no exclamation marks, no cheerleading.
32	
33	## Anti-references
34	
35	- **Gmail-web clutter:** toolbars of rarely-used icons, chrome competing with content, permanent competing panels.
36	- **"AI magic" email products:** AI destinations, sparkle icons, generated summaries presented as fact, fabricated contact enrichment, automation that acts without a preview.
37	- **Superhuman feature-parity clone:** Superhuman is the visual and interaction reference for browsing (layout, density, type, keyboard feel), and close look parity there is a goal. Features and workflows are our own; don't import Superhuman's product scope or claim verified behavioral parity.
38	- **Generic SaaS dashboard aesthetics:** card stacks and grids, gradient heroes, oversized rounded panels, decorative illustration or motion.
39	- **Optimistic UI that lies:** "Done" before the provider confirmed, silent retries of ambiguous sends, dead controls that look actionable.
40	
41	## Design Principles
42	
43	1. **Honest state over smooth feel.** When speed and truthfulness conflict, show the truth. Every action has a visible pending, success, partial, failed, or unknown state. Show evidence and coverage, including unknown and retained facts.
44	2. **Keyboard first, mouse welcome.** Every core triage path is reachable and discoverable from the keyboard; pointer interaction is supported, never required.
45	3. **Content is the interface.** Chrome stays quiet and compact so the list and the conversation dominate. Add UI only when it earns its space in the triage loop; reuse established commands, navigation and recovery surfaces before adding new ones.
46	4. **Preview before power.** Bulk actions, automations, and agent-proposed changes show what they will do before they do it, and report exactly what they did after. Focus, bulk selection and message identity stay separate concepts.
47	5. **Opinionated defaults, replaceable parts.** Ship one strong way of working; design surfaces so views, signals, and commands can be swapped without breaking the core experience.
48	
49	Standing constraints: ordinary reading stays local and non-mutating; message content renders as safe literal plain text; drafts stay local-only.
50	
51	## Accessibility & Inclusion
52	
53	Not a formal priority at this stage; no WCAG conformance target or certification is implied. Keyboard operability and visible focus remain required because they are core to the keyboard-first model. Don't regress behavior that already exists (explicit action labels, editable/IME shortcut protection, reduced-motion alternatives, selection/outcome announcements). The existing desktop/contact breakpoints remain authoritative; no new mobile UI. Revisit if the audience expands beyond the author.

207	# Design System: Email OS
208	
209	## 1. Overview
210	
211	**Creative North Star: "The Quiet Instrument"**
212	
213	A precision tool used in long, focused sessions. The surface is a single warm charcoal plane. The interface recedes until only the list, the open conversation and the next decision are on screen. Density is high but calm: 36px rows, small type, no dividers, no cards. One violet signal marks where you are. Everything else is a tonal step on the same warm gray ramp.
214	
215	The system follows Superhuman's browsing look closely, and that parity is an explicit goal. It covers geometry, density, type scale, tonal layering and the focused-row treatment. Features and workflows stay our own. The one place we deliberately go our own way is state: pending, failed, partial and outcome-unknown states are always visible in their own form (*"Honest state over smooth feel"*, PRODUCT.md). A quiet surface must never hide what happened.
216	
217	The system rejects Gmail-web clutter, "AI magic" sparkle chrome, generic SaaS dashboards (card grids, gradient heroes, oversized rounded panels), and optimistic UI that says "Done" before the provider confirms.
218	
219	**Key Characteristics:**
220	- Three fixed panes: a 40px icon rail, a fluid list or reader, and a 272px darker contact pane. Each is separated by a single 1px divider.

276	## 2. Colors
277	
278	One warm charcoal ramp, one violet signal, and two status hues reserved for truth-telling.
279	
280	### Primary
281	- **Dusk Lavender** (`focus-accent`): the single "you are here" signal. Used for the 4px bar on the focused row, the active message bar in the reader, focus outlines, and the highlighted command. It never fills an area and never decorates.
282	
283	### Secondary
284	- **Orchid Dot** (`unread-marker`): only for the 5px unread dot in the row gutter. It is pinker than Dusk Lavender so that unread and focus never read as the same signal.
285	
286	### Neutral
287	- **Warm Charcoal** (`surface`): the list, rail and header plane. Everything sits on it.
288	- **Deep Umber** (`surface-contact`): the contact pane and utility drawers. It is one step darker, so context reads as secondary to the list.
289	- **Lifted Charcoal** (`surface-raised`): utility chips, overlays and inputs.
290	- **Focus Stone** (`focus-fill`): the focused-row and active-message fill, and the highlighted command item.
291	- **Inkwell** (`rail-well`): the pill behind the rail's navigation glyphs.
292	- **Rail Pebble** (`rail-button`): the circular rail action button.
293	- **Paper White** (`text-primary`): sender, subject, active tab, contact name and email, labels.
294	- **Ash** (`text-secondary`): snippet, date, group caption, contact threads, counts.
295	- **Smoke** (`text-tertiary`): inactive split tabs.
296	- **Graphite** (`icon-muted`): every resting glyph (row actions, compose, search, hamburger, footer icons, attachment). Hover and focus raise glyphs to Paper White.
297	- **Seam** (`divider`): the 1px vertical separators between rail, list and contact pane. Nothing else.
298	
299	### Status
300	- **Amber Notice** (`warning`): pending, outcome unknown, local-only, expired-undo and partial states.
301	- **Coral Fault** (`danger`): confirmed failures and command errors.
302	
303	### Named Rules
304	**The One Signal Rule.** Dusk Lavender appears at most once per screen, on the current row or message. If two violet things are visible, one of them is wrong.
305	
306	**The Seams-Only Rule.** Dividers separate panes, never rows. Rows are separated by rhythm alone.
307	
308	**The Status-Is-Sacred Rule.** Amber and coral are never used decoratively, and a status is never shown only as a tint: every status carries words.
309	
310	## 3. Typography
311	
312	**Body Font:** system-ui (with -apple-system, sans-serif)
313	**Label/Mono Font:** ui-monospace, for plain-text message bodies only
314	
315	**Character:** One local system sans in two weights carries the whole UI. Hierarchy comes from weight (600 vs 400) and tone (Paper White vs Ash), not size. The browsing shell uses just two sizes.
316	
317	### Hierarchy
318	- **Headline** (400, 1rem / 16px, 1.25): split tabs and the contact name. This is the only large text in the shell.
319	- **Title** (600, 0.75rem / 12px, 1.35): sender names, contact email, section labels ("Mail"), footer labels, notice labels.
320	- **Body** (400, 0.75rem / 12px, 1.35): subject (Paper White), snippet and threads (Ash), date-group captions (Ash).
321	- **Label** (400, 0.75rem / 12px, tabular numerals): dates ("8:00 AM", "6 NOV" with an uppercase month) and counts in status text.
322	- **Mono** and the other steps are CSS tokens: `--type-headline`, `--type-body`, `--type-count`, `--type-mono`, `--weight-regular`, `--weight-strong` (`src/assets/style.css`). Use the tokens, never a literal size.
323	
324	### Dates
325	Row and reader dates are one fixed product format, not a locale format. They depend only on the instant, the current time and the viewer's time zone (`src/lib/browsing-dates.ts`). Month group captions ("October 2026") still follow the locale.
326	- **Row, today:** the time, 12-hour, no leading zero: "8:00 AM", "12:05 PM".
327	- **Row, earlier this calendar year:** day and month: "6 NOV". The DOM text is "6 Nov"; CSS uppercases it, so screen readers hear a word, not letters.
328	- **Row, any other year (past or future):** day, month and four-digit year: "9 JAN 2025". The day is kept for precision, and a two-digit year would read as another day.
329	- **Unknown or unparsable:** "Unknown" in the row, "Unknown date" in full form. Never blank.
330	- **Full form** (reader message times, the row date's hover title): "Thu 9 Jan 2025, 6:29 PM". The same 12-hour clock as the row.
331	- Every rendered date is a `<time>` with a normalized ISO `datetime` when the timestamp parses.
332	- **Count** (400, 0.6875rem / 11px): split-tab counts, set 4px after the tab label.
333	- **Mono** (400, 0.85rem, 1.45): the current plain-text message body in the reader.
334	
335	Sizes are rem so the 16px and 20px root-font layouts in `tests/inbox-list.rendered-layout.test.ts` still scale. Row and header heights are min-heights in px. The 12px row size is measured from the capture: system-ui glyph metrics point to 11.5–12px.
336	
337	### Named Rules
338	**The Two-Size Rule.** The browsing shell uses 16px and 12px only (11px for counts). A third size in the list needs a written reason.
339	
340	**The No-Caps-Caption Rule.** No uppercase letter-spaced captions in the browsing shell. Date groups and pane headings are title case. Uppercase is allowed only for the month in compact dates.
341	
342	## 4. Elevation
343	
344	The browsing shell is flat. Depth comes from tonal layering: Warm Charcoal for the plane, Deep Umber for context, Focus Stone for the current row, Inkwell for the rail well. No shadows sit on rows, panes, the header or the rail. Shadows appear only on surfaces that truly float above the shell and cover it.
345	
346	### Shadow Vocabulary
347	- **Drawer cast** (`box-shadow: -8px 0 24px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.35)`): the right-edge utility drawer (Activity, Account, Drafts).
348	- **Popover lift** (`box-shadow: 0 6px 16px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.35)`): the compact row-actions disclosure panel.
349	- **Overlay lift** (`box-shadow: 0 16px 64px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.53)`): the command palette and navigator, over a `#00000088` backdrop.
350	
351	### Named Rules
352	**The Flat-Shell Rule.** If something in the rail, header, list or contact pane casts a shadow, remove it. Shadows mean "this covers the shell", nothing else.
353	
354	## 5. Components
355	
356	### Conversation Row (signature)
357	The core of the product: dense, quiet and exact.
358	- **Shape:** square corners (0), a fixed 36px height, inset 6px from both pane edges.
359	- **Layout:** a 44px gutter (unread dot, or the checkbox in selection mode), then a 132px sender (Title, Paper White, ellipsis), then the subject (Body, Paper White) and snippet (Body, Ash) on one line with 12px gaps, then the trailing date (Label, Ash) about 25px from the pane edge. An attachment glyph (Graphite, 16px) sits before the date when present.
360	- **Focused:** Focus Stone fill plus a 4px Dusk Lavender bar on the fill's own left edge. The date gives way to three action glyphs (done, snooze, more) at a 32px pitch.
361	- **Hover:** a barely-there lift (`rgba(255,255,255,0.03)`). Action glyphs appear; focus and read state never change.
362	- **Pending / unknown:** an Amber Notice word ("Pending…") in the meta region, never just a tint.
363	- **Selected:** the visible checkbox plus a secondary inset bar, so selection never relies on color alone and never replaces the focus bar.
364	
365	### Date Group Caption
366	- **Style:** Body, Ash, title case ("Yesterday"), on the 50px content inset, in a 48px block. No rule and no background band. Not focusable.
367	
368	### Split Tabs (Navigation)
369	- **Style:** Headline type. The active tab is Paper White; inactive tabs are Smoke. The count (11px, Ash) follows 4px after the label and disappears at zero. Tabs are spaced 18px apart.
370	- **Header:** 78px tall, no bottom border. The hamburger is a Graphite glyph to the left of the inset; compose and search are Graphite glyphs on the right, at the row-action pitch.
371	
372	### Rail
373	- **Style:** 40px wide on Warm Charcoal, with a 1px Seam on its right. The top action, Inbox, is a 28px Rail Pebble circle centered on the tab line. The other destination glyphs sit in a 30px Inkwell pill at a 28px pitch, with the first glyph on the first list line. Utilities (Account, Activity, Drafts, and Contact below 1000px) are ghost glyphs at the bottom. The active destination glyph is Paper White on a 24px Rail Pebble disc; the rest are Graphite.
374	- **Labels:** icon-only on screen. Every button keeps its text label as its accessible name, a `title`, and a keyboard tooltip on `:focus-visible`.
375	- **Activity badge:** an Amber Notice count of unresolved operations (pending plus outcome unknown), named in words by the button's description and title.
376	
377	### Contact Pane
378	- **Style:** 272px on Deep Umber, with a 1px Seam on its left and a 24px inset. No visible caption heading (it stays for assistive tech).
379	- **Content:** the name in Headline on the tab line; the email in Title on the first list line; copy glyphs in each line's trailing slot, revealed on hover or focus; a section label (Title with a 16px glyph) followed by recent threads (Body, Ash, ellipsis, 24px pitch); exact known data only, never invented enrichment.
380	- **Footer:** none. Superhuman's footer toolbar has no counterpart with real actions here; the utilities live in the rail (Parity gap 9).
381	
382	### Buttons
383	- **Ghost (browsing shell):** transparent, Paper White Title text or a Graphite glyph, 4px radius, `2px 8px`. On hover or focus, the glyph rises to Paper White; the focus ring is a 2px Dusk Lavender outline at a 1px offset.
384	- **Utility (drawers, recovery banners):** a Lifted Charcoal fill with a 1px Seam border, 4px radius, `2px 8px`. This is the only bordered button.
385	
386	### Command Overlay
387	- **Style:** a Lifted Charcoal panel, 10px radius, 576px max width, Overlay lift, 15vh from the top. The input sits on Deep Umber with a 1px Dusk Lavender border. The highlighted item gets a Focus Stone fill plus a 3px Dusk Lavender left bar. Shortcuts are shown as `kbd` in Ash.
388	
389	### Inputs / Fields
390	- **Style:** a Lifted Charcoal fill, a 1px Seam border, 4px radius, inherited font.
391	- **Focus:** the border shifts to Dusk Lavender. No glow.
392	
393	### In-flow Notices (Action notice, Selection bar, coverage and recovery)
394	- **Style:** borderless strips in normal flow above the list, aligned to the 50px content inset, in Body type. Status words use Amber Notice or Coral Fault. Undo shows its `kbd` hint in Ash. They never overlay rows and never auto-hide a failure.
395	
396	## 6. Do's and Don'ts
397	
398	### Do:
399	- **Do** keep rows at exactly 36px with 12px type, and separate them by rhythm alone.
400	- **Do** align split tabs, sender names, date captions and notices to the single 50px content inset.
401	- **Do** use Dusk Lavender (#bba5ed) only for the current row or message, and the focus ring.
402	- **Do** show every pending, partial, failed and outcome-unknown state in words, in Amber Notice or Coral Fault, where the user is already looking.
403	- **Do** align the contact pane to the list: the name on the tab line, the email on the first-row line.
404	- **Do** ship glyphs as local inline SVG with an accessible name. No icon fonts and no CDN.
405	- **Do** treat Superhuman's browsing look as the visual and interaction reference. Close look parity is the goal (PRODUCT.md).
406	
407	### Don't:
408	- **Don't** draw dividers between rows or under the header. Seams separate panes only.
409	- **Don't** use uppercase letter-spaced captions in the browsing shell.
410	- **Don't** add Gmail-web clutter: toolbars of rarely-used icons, or chrome competing with content.
411	- **Don't** add "AI magic" chrome: sparkle icons, or generated summaries presented as fact.
412	- **Don't** build a Superhuman feature-parity clone. Copy the browsing look, not Superhuman's product scope.
413	- **Don't** use generic SaaS dashboard aesthetics: card grids, gradient heroes, oversized rounded panels, decorative illustration.
414	- **Don't** show optimistic UI that lies: no "Done" toast before the provider confirms, and no silent retry of an ambiguous send.
415	- **Don't** put shadows on anything in the rail, header, list or contact pane.
416	- **Don't** introduce a third type size in the list, or use off-palette hex values (the old command-overlay violets are the cautionary example).
417	- **Don't** load remote fonts, images or CDN assets.

23	## Design guidance
24	
25	Produce ready-to-ship, production-grade code, not prototypes or starting points. Take no shortcuts unless the user asks for them (when in doubt, ask). Don't stop until arriving at a complete implementation (beautiful, responsive, fast, precise, bug-free, on brand). You take attention to detail seriously: every page, section or component crafted is battle tested using the tools available to you (browser screenshotting, computer use, etc). the model is capable of extraordinary work. Don't hold back.
26	
27	### General rules
28	
29	#### Color
30	
31	- **Verify contrast.** Body text must hit ≥4.5:1 against its background; large text (≥18px or bold ≥14px) needs ≥3:1. Placeholder text needs the same 4.5:1, not the muted-gray default. The most common failure: muted gray body text on a tinted near-white. If the contrast is even close, bump the body color toward the ink end of the ramp; light gray "for elegance" is the single biggest reason AI designs feel hard to read.
32	- Gray text on a colored background looks washed out. Use a darker shade of the background's own hue, or a transparency of the text color.
33	
34	#### Typography
35	
36	- Cap body line length at 65–75ch.
37	- Don't pair fonts that are similar but not identical (two geometric sans-serifs, two humanist sans-serifs). Pair on a contrast axis (serif + sans, geometric + humanist) or use one family in multiple weights.
38	- Hero / display heading ceiling: clamp() max ≤ 6rem (~96px). Above that the page is shouting, not designing.
39	- Display heading letter-spacing floor: ≥ -0.04em. Anything tighter and letters touch; cramped, not "designed".
40	- Use `text-wrap: balance` on h1–h3 for even line lengths; `text-wrap: pretty` on long prose to reduce orphans.
41	
42	#### Layout
43	
44	- Vary spacing for rhythm.
45	- Cards are the lazy answer. Use them only when they're truly the best affordance. Nested cards are always wrong.
46	- Flexbox for 1D, Grid for 2D. Don't default to Grid when `flex-wrap` would be simpler.
47	- For responsive grids without breakpoints: `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr))`.
48	- Build a semantic z-index scale (dropdown → sticky → modal-backdrop → modal → toast → tooltip). Never arbitrary values like 999 or 9999.
49	
50	#### Motion
51	- Motion should be intentional, and not be an afterthought. consider it as part of the build.
52	- Don't animate CSS layout properties unless truly needed.
53	- Ease out with exponential curves (ease-out-quart / quint / expo). No bounce, no elastic.
54	- Use libraries for more advanced motion needs (e.g. motion, gsap, anime.js, lenis etc)
55	- Reduced motion is not optional. Every animation needs a `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` alternative: typically a crossfade or instant transition.
56	- Staggering the items within one list is legitimate. The tell is the uniform reflex (one identical entrance applied to every section), not motion itself; each reveal should fit what it reveals. Suppressing the reflex is never a reason to ship a page with no motion at all.
57	- Reveal animations must enhance an already-visible default. Don't gate content visibility on a class-triggered transition; transitions pause on hidden tabs and headless renderers, so the reveal never fires and the section ships blank.
58	- Premium motion materials are not just transform/opacity. Blur, backdrop-filter, clip-path, mask, and shadow/glow are part of the palette when they materially improve the effect and stay smooth.
59	
60	#### Interaction
61	
62	- Dropdowns rendered with `position: absolute` inside an `overflow: hidden` or `overflow: auto` container will be clipped. Use the native `<dialog>` / popover API, `position: fixed`, or a portal to escape the stacking context.
63	
64	### New projects only (when no prior work exists)
65	
66	#### Color & Theme
67	
68	- Use OKLCH.
69	- **The cream / sand / beige body bg is the saturated AI default of 2026.** The whole warm-neutral band (OKLCH L 0.84-0.97, C < 0.06, hue 40-100) reads as cream/sand/paper/parchment regardless of what you call it. Token names like `--paper`, `--cream`, `--sand`, `--bone`, `--flour`, `--linen`, `--parchment`, `--wheat`, `--biscuit`, `--ivory` are tells in themselves. If the brief is "warm, traditional, family-coastal-Italian" or "magazine-warm" or "editorial-restraint", DO NOT translate that into a near-white warm-tinted bg; that's the AI move. Pick: (a) a saturated brand color as the body (terracotta, oxblood, deep ochre, near-black), (b) a true off-white at chroma 0 (or chroma toward the brand's own hue, not toward warmth-by-default), or (c) a darker mid-tone tinted neutral that's clearly the brand's own. "Warmth" in the brand is carried by accent + typography + imagery, not by body bg.
70	- Tinted neutrals: add 0.005–0.015 chroma toward the brand's hue. Don't default-tint toward warm or cool "because the brand feels that way"; that's the cross-project monoculture move.
71	- When picking a theme: Dark vs. light is never a default. Not dark "because tools look cool dark." Not light "to be safe.".Before choosing, write one sentence of physical scene: who uses this, where, under what ambient light, in what mood. If the sentence doesn't force the answer, it's not concrete enough. Add detail until it does.
72	- Pick a **color strategy** before picking colors. Four steps on the commitment axis:
73	  - **Restrained**: tinted neutrals + one accent ≤10%. Product default; brand minimalism.
74	  - **Committed**: one saturated color carries 30–60% of the surface. Brand default for identity-driven pages.
75	  - **Full palette**: 3–4 named roles, each used deliberately. Brand campaigns; product data viz.
76	  - **Drenched**: the surface IS the color. Brand heroes, campaign pages.
77	
78	### Absolute bans
79	
80	Match-and-refuse. If you're about to write any of these, rewrite the element with different structure.
81	
82	- **Side-stripe borders.** `border-left` or `border-right` greater than 1px as a colored accent on cards, list items, callouts, or alerts. Never intentional. Rewrite with full borders, background tints, leading numbers/icons, or nothing.
83	- **Gradient text.** `background-clip: text` combined with a gradient background. Decorative, never meaningful. Use a single solid color. Emphasis via weight or size.
84	- **Glassmorphism as default.** Blurs and glass cards used decoratively. Rare and purposeful, or nothing.
85	- **The hero-metric template.** Big number, small label, supporting stats, gradient accent. SaaS cliché.
86	- **Identical card grids.** Same-sized cards with icon + heading + text, repeated endlessly.
87	- **Tiny uppercase tracked eyebrow above every section.** The 2023-era kicker (small all-caps text with wide tracking, "ABOUT" "PROCESS" "PRICING" above each heading) is now the saturated AI scaffold; it appears on 55-95% of generations regardless of brief, which is the definition of a tell. One named kicker as a deliberate brand system is voice; an eyebrow on every section is AI grammar. Choose a different cadence.
88	- **Numbered section markers as default scaffolding (01 / 02 / 03).** Putting `01 · About / 02 · Process / 03 · Pricing` above every section is the eyebrow trope one tier deeper: reach for it because "landing pages do this" and you're scaffolding by reflex. Numbers earn their place when the section actually IS a sequence (a real 3-step process, an ordered flow, a typed timeline) and the order carries information the reader needs. One deliberate numbered sequence on one page is voice; numbered eyebrows on every section across the site is AI grammar.
89	- **Text that overflows its container.** Long heading words plus large clamp scales plus narrow grids cause headline overflow on tablet/mobile. Test the heading copy at every breakpoint; if it overflows, reduce the clamp max or rewrite the copy. The viewport is part of the design.
90	
91	### The AI slop test
92	
93	If someone could look at this interface and say "AI made that" without doubt, it's failed. Cross-register failures are the absolute bans above. Register-specific failures live in each reference.
94	
95	**Category-reflex check.** Run at two altitudes; the second one catches what the first one misses.
96	
97	- **First-order:** if someone could guess the theme + palette from the category alone, it's the first training-data reflex. Rework the scene sentence and color strategy until the answer isn't obvious from the domain.
98	- **Second-order:** if someone could guess the aesthetic family from category-plus-anti-references ("AI workflow tool that's not SaaS-cream → editorial-typographic", "fintech that's not navy-and-gold → terminal-native dark mode"), it's the trap one tier deeper. The first reflex was avoided; the second wasn't. Rework until both answers are not obvious. The brand register's [reflex-reject aesthetic lanes](reference/brand.md) list catches the currently-saturated families.

173	## Design System Discovery
174	
175	Aligning the feature to the design system is **not optional**. Polish without alignment is decoration on top of drift, and it makes the next person's job harder. Discovery comes before any other polish work.
176	
177	1. **Find the design system**: Search for design system documentation, component libraries, style guides, or token definitions. Study the core patterns: design principles, target audience, color tokens, spacing scale, typography styles, component API, motion conventions.
178	2. **Note the conventions**: How are shared components imported? What spacing scale is used? Which colors come from tokens vs hard-coded values? What motion and interaction patterns are established? What flow shapes are used for comparable actions (modal vs full-page, inline vs route, save-on-blur vs explicit submit)?
179	3. **Identify drift, then name the root cause**: For every deviation, classify it as a **missing token** (the value should exist in the system but doesn't), a **one-off implementation** (a shared component already exists but wasn't used), or a **conceptual misalignment** (the feature's flow, IA, or hierarchy doesn't match neighboring features). The fix differs by category: patch the value, swap to the shared component, or rework the flow. Fixing the symptom without naming the cause is how drift compounds.
180	
181	If a design system exists, polish **must** align the feature with it. If none exists, polish against the conventions visible in the codebase. **If anything about the system is ambiguous, ask. Never guess at design system principles.**

184

191	   - When does it ship? (How much time for polish?)

193	2. **Think experience-first**: Who actually uses this, and what's the best possible experience for them? Effective design beats decorative polish; a feature that looks beautiful but fights the user's flow is not polished. Walk the path from their perspective before opening DevTools.
194	
195	3. **Identify polish areas**:
196	   - Visual inconsistencies
197	   - Spacing and alignment issues
198	   - Interaction state gaps
199	   - Copy inconsistencies
200	   - Edge cases and error states
201	   - Loading and transition smoothness
202	   - Information architecture and flow drift (does this feature reveal complexity the way neighboring features do?)

204	4. **Pull in any prior critique** (optional signal): If `/impeccable critique` has been run on the same target, its priority issues are a useful prior for what to address first. Resolve the target to a file path or URL, then:

207	   node .pi/skills/impeccable/scripts/critique-storage.mjs latest "$slug"

When polish time is tight, functional issues ship first; cosmetic ones can land in a follow-up. Quality should be consistent; never perfect one corner while leaving another rough.

215	## Polish Systematically
216	
217	Work through these dimensions methodically:
218	
219	### Visual Alignment & Spacing
220	
221	- **Pixel-perfect alignment**: Everything lines up to grid
222	- **Consistent spacing**: All gaps use spacing scale (no random 13px gaps)
223	- **Optical alignment**: Adjust for visual weight (icons may need offset for optical centering)
224	- **Responsive consistency**: Spacing and alignment work at all breakpoints
225	- **Grid adherence**: Elements snap to baseline grid
226	
227	**Check**:
228	- Enable grid overlay and verify alignment
229	- Check spacing with browser inspector
230	- Test at multiple viewport sizes
231	- Look for elements that "feel" off
232	
233	### Information Architecture & Flow
234	
235	Visual polish on a misshapen flow is wasted work. Match the *shape* of the experience to the system, not just the surface.
236	
237	- **Progressive disclosure**: Match how much is revealed when, compared to neighboring features. A settings page exposing 40 fields when the rest of the app reveals 5 at a time is drift, even if every field is perfectly styled.
238	- **Established user flows**: Multi-step actions follow the same shape as comparable flows elsewhere: modal vs full-page, inline edit vs separate route, save-on-blur vs explicit submit, optimistic vs pessimistic updates.
239	- **Hierarchy & complexity**: The same conceptual weight gets the same visual weight throughout. Primary actions don't become tertiary in one corner of the product, and tertiary actions don't shout.
240	- **Empty, loading, and arrival transitions**: How content arrives, updates, and leaves matches how it does in adjacent features.
241	- **Naming and mental model**: The feature uses the same nouns and verbs as the rest of the system. A "Workspace" here shouldn't be a "Project" three screens away.
242	
243	### Typography Refinement
244	
245	- **Hierarchy consistency**: Same elements use same sizes/weights throughout
246	- **Line length**: 45-75 characters for body text
247	- **Line height**: Appropriate for font size and context
248	- **Widows & orphans**: No single words on last line
249	- **Hyphenation**: Appropriate for language and column width
250	- **Kerning**: Adjust letter spacing where needed (especially headlines)
251	- **Font loading**: No FOUT/FOIT flashes
252	
253	### Color & Contrast
254	
255	- **Contrast ratios**: All text meets WCAG standards
256	- **Consistent token usage**: No hard-coded colors, all use design tokens
257	- **Theme consistency**: Works in all theme variants
258	- **Color meaning**: Same colors mean same things throughout
259	- **Accessible focus**: Focus indicators visible with sufficient contrast
260	- **Gray on color**: Never put gray text on colored backgrounds; use a shade of that color or transparency
261	
262	### Interaction States
263	
264	Every interactive element needs all states:
265	
266	- **Default**: Resting state
267	- **Hover**: Subtle feedback (color, scale, shadow)
268	- **Focus**: Keyboard focus indicator (never remove without replacement)
269	- **Active**: Click/tap feedback
270	- **Disabled**: Clearly non-interactive
271	- **Loading**: Async action feedback
272	- **Error**: Validation or error state
273	- **Success**: Successful completion
274	
275	**Missing states create confusion and broken experiences**.
276	
277	### Micro-interactions & Transitions
278	
279	- **Smooth transitions**: All state changes animated appropriately (150-300ms)
280	- **Consistent easing**: Use ease-out-quart/quint/expo for natural deceleration. Never bounce or elastic; they feel dated.
281	- **No jank**: Smooth animations; use atmospheric blur/filter/mask/shadow effects when they add polish, but bound expensive paint areas and avoid casual layout-property animation
282	- **Appropriate motion**: Motion serves purpose, not decoration
283	- **Reduced motion**: Respects `prefers-reduced-motion`
284	
285	### Content & Copy
286	
287	- **Consistent terminology**: Same things called same names throughout
288	- **Consistent capitalization**: Title Case vs Sentence case applied consistently
289	- **Grammar & spelling**: No typos
290	- **Appropriate length**: Not too wordy, not too terse
291	- **Punctuation consistency**: Periods on sentences, not on labels (unless all labels have them)
292	
293	### Icons & Images
294	
295	- **Consistent style**: All icons from same family or matching style
296	- **Appropriate sizing**: Icons sized consistently for context
297	- **Proper alignment**: Icons align with adjacent text optically
298	- **Alt text**: All images have descriptive alt text
299	- **Loading states**: Images don't cause layout shift, proper aspect ratios
300	- **Retina support**: 2x assets for high-DPI screens
301	
302	### Forms & Inputs
303	
304	- **Label consistency**: All inputs properly labeled
305	- **Required indicators**: Clear and consistent
306	- **Error messages**: Helpful and consistent
307	- **Tab order**: Logical keyboard navigation
308	- **Auto-focus**: Appropriate (don't overuse)
309	- **Validation timing**: Consistent (on blur vs on submit)
310	
311	### Edge Cases & Error States
312	
313	- **Loading states**: All async actions have loading feedback
314	- **Empty states**: Helpful empty states, not just blank space
315	- **Error states**: Clear error messages with recovery paths
316	- **Success states**: Confirmation of successful actions
317	- **Long content**: Handles very long names, descriptions, etc.
318	- **No content**: Handles missing data gracefully
319	- **Offline**: Appropriate offline handling (if applicable)
320	
321	### Responsiveness
322	
323	- **All breakpoints**: Test mobile, tablet, desktop
324	- **Touch targets**: 44x44px minimum on touch devices
325	- **Readable text**: No text smaller than 14px on mobile
326	- **No horizontal scroll**: Content fits viewport
327	- **Appropriate reflow**: Content adapts logically
328	
329	### Performance
330	
331	- **Fast initial load**: Optimize critical path
332	- **No layout shift**: Elements don't jump after load (CLS)
333	- **Smooth interactions**: No lag or jank
334	- **Optimized images**: Appropriate formats and sizes
335	- **Lazy loading**: Off-screen content loads lazily
336	
337	### Code Quality
338	
339	- **Remove console logs**: No debug logging in production
340	- **Remove commented code**: Clean up dead code
341	- **Remove unused imports**: Clean up unused dependencies
342	- **Consistent naming**: Variables and functions follow conventions
343	- **Type safety**: No TypeScript `any` or ignored errors
344	- **Accessibility**: Proper ARIA labels and semantic HTML
345	
346	## Polish Checklist
347	
348	Go through systematically:
349	
350	- [ ] Aligned to the design system (drift named and resolved by root cause)
351	- [ ] Information architecture and flow shape match neighboring features
352	- [ ] Visual alignment perfect at all breakpoints
353	- [ ] Spacing uses design tokens consistently
354	- [ ] Typography hierarchy consistent
355	- [ ] All interactive states implemented
356	- [ ] All transitions smooth (60fps)
357	- [ ] Copy is consistent and polished
358	- [ ] Icons are consistent and properly sized
359	- [ ] All forms properly labeled and validated
360	- [ ] Error states are helpful
361	- [ ] Loading states are clear
362	- [ ] Empty states are welcoming
363	- [ ] Touch targets are 44x44px minimum
364	- [ ] Contrast ratios meet WCAG AA
365	- [ ] Keyboard navigation works
366	- [ ] Focus indicators visible
367	- [ ] No console errors or warnings
368	- [ ] No layout shift on load
369	- [ ] Works in all supported browsers
370	- [ ] Respects reduced motion preference
371	- [ ] Code is clean (no TODOs, console.logs, commented code)
372	
373	**IMPORTANT**: Polish is about details. Zoom in. Squint at it. Use it yourself. The little things add up.
374	
375	Sweat the details. Zoom in until the alignment is right and the spacing reads as deliberate. Then ship.
376	
377	**NEVER**:
378	- Polish before it's functionally complete
379	- Polish without aligning to the design system; that's decoration on drift
380	- Guess at design system principles instead of asking when something is ambiguous
381	- Spend hours on polish if it ships in 30 minutes (triage)
382	- Introduce bugs while polishing (test thoroughly)
383	- Ignore systematic issues (if spacing is off everywhere, fix the system, not just one screen)
384	- Perfect one thing while leaving others rough (consistent quality level)
385	- Create new one-off components when design system equivalents exist
386	- Hard-code values that should use design tokens
387	- Introduce new patterns or flows that diverge from established ones
388	
389	## Final Verification
390	
391	Before marking as done:
392	
393	- **Use it yourself**: Actually interact with the feature.
394	- **Test on real devices**: Not just browser DevTools.
395	- **Ask someone else to review**: Fresh eyes catch things.
396	- **Compare to design**: Match intended design.
397	- **Check all states**: Don't just test happy path.
398	- **Treat automation carefully**: Run detector or QA commands when they are available and relevant, fix their defects, but never cite a clean result as proof that the work is polished.
399	
400	## Clean Up
401	
402	After polishing, ensure code quality:
403	
404	- **Replace custom implementations**: If the design system provides a component you reimplemented, switch to the shared version.
405	- **Remove orphaned code**: Delete unused styles, components, or files made obsolete by polish.
406	- **Consolidate tokens**: If you introduced new values, check whether they should be tokens.
407	- **Verify DRYness**: Look for duplication introduced during polishing and consolidate.
408	# Product register
409	
410	When design SERVES the product: app UIs, admin dashboards, settings panels, data tables, tools, authenticated surfaces, anything where the user is in a task.
411	
412	## The product slop test
413	
414	Not "would someone say AI made this." Familiarity is often a feature here. The test is: would a user fluent in the category's best tools (Linear, Figma, Notion, Raycast, Stripe come to mind) sit down and trust this interface, or pause at every subtly-off component?
415	
416	Product UI's failure mode isn't flatness, it's strangeness without purpose: over-decorated buttons, mismatched form controls, gratuitous motion, display fonts where labels should be, invented affordances for standard tasks. The bar is earned familiarity. The tool should disappear into the task.
417	
418	## Typography
419	
420	- **One family is often right.** Product UIs don't need display/body pairing. A well-tuned sans carries headings, buttons, labels, body, data.
421	- **Fixed rem scale, not fluid.** Clamp-sized headings don't serve product UI. Users view at consistent DPI, and a fluid h1 that shrinks in a sidebar looks worse, not better.
422	- **Tighter scale ratio.** 1.125–1.2 between steps is typical. More type elements here than on brand surfaces; exaggerated contrast creates noise.
423	- **Line length still applies for prose** (65–75ch). Data and compact UI can run denser; tables at 120ch+ are fine.
424	
425	## Color
426	
427	Product defaults to Restrained. A single surface can earn Committed (a dashboard where one category color carries a report, an onboarding flow with a drenched welcome screen), but Restrained is the floor.
428	
429	- State-rich semantic vocabulary: hover, focus, active, disabled, selected, loading, error, warning, success, info. Standardize these.
430	- Accent color used for primary actions, current selection, and state indicators only, not decoration.
431	- A second neutral layer for sidebars, toolbars, and panels (slightly cooler or warmer than the content surface).
432	
433	## Layout
434	
435	- Responsive behavior is structural (collapse sidebar, responsive table, breakpoint-driven columns), not fluid typography.
436	
437	## Components
438	
439	Every interactive component has: default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error. Don't ship with half of these.
440	
441	- Skeleton states for loading, not spinners in the middle of content.
442	- Empty states that teach the interface, not "nothing here."
443	- Consistent affordances across the surface. Same button shape. Same form-control vocabulary. Same icon style.
444	
445	## Motion
446	
447	- 150–250 ms on most transitions. Users are in flow; don't make them wait for choreography.
448	- Motion conveys state, not decoration. State change, feedback, loading, reveal: nothing else.
449	- No orchestrated page-load sequences. Product loads into a task; users don't want to watch it load.
450	
451	## Product bans (on top of the shared absolute bans)
452	
453	- Decorative motion that doesn't convey state.
454	- Inconsistent component vocabulary across screens. If the "save" button looks different in two places, one is wrong.
455	- Display fonts in UI labels, buttons, data.
456	- Reinventing standard affordances for flavor (custom scrollbars, weird form controls, non-standard modals).
457	- Heavy color or full-saturation accents on inactive states.
458	- Modal as first thought. Modals are usually laziness. Exhaust inline / progressive alternatives first.
459	
460	## Product permissions
461	
462	Product can afford things brand surfaces can't.
463	
464	- System fonts and familiar sans defaults (Inter, SF Pro, system-ui stacks).
465	- Standard navigation patterns: top bar + side nav, breadcrumbs, tabs, command palettes.
466	- Density. Tables with many rows, panels with many labels, dense information when users need it.
467	- Consistency over surprise. The same visual vocabulary screen to screen is a virtue; delight is saved for moments, not pages.

7	## Users
8	
9	Initially a single person: the author, dogfooding a single-account desktop client (macOS first) against their own Gmail inbox in focused, keyboard-first sessions. They move through a high volume of mail quickly, want to reach "done" on each conversation, and need to trust that every action (archive, bulk processing, undo, send) did exactly what it claimed. The provider's own client remains the fallback.
10	
11	Longer term: technically capable people who want to compose their own email workflow (custom views, triage signals, commands, automations), manually or with an agent, without rebuilding sync, credentials, or send safety.
12	
13	The primary task on most screens is triage: scan the list, open a conversation, decide, act, move on.
14	
15	## Product Purpose
16	
17	A composable email client: a trusted mail engine (sync, safe rendering, credentials, action execution) with replaceable signals, views, commands, and workflows on top. It ships an opinionated reference experience, a compact Superhuman-style browsing and keyboard flow, rather than a blank toolkit.
18	
19	The near-term goal is a complete, trustworthy inbox-processing session. Strategic scope is set by `docs/adr/0001-single-account-desktop-email-client.md` and `superhuman-email-browsing-ux-spec.md`; this file does not expand it.
20	
21	Success looks like: the author processes their inbox faster and with more confidence than in their previous client, and every automated or bulk action is previewable, reported honestly (including partial success and "outcome unknown"), and undoable where undo is real.
22	
23	## Brand Personality
24	
25	**Focused, precise, trustworthy.**
26	
27	- **Focused:** the interface recedes so the mail and the next decision are what's on screen. Dense, quiet, few competing elements.
28	- **Precise:** exact states, exact counts, exact wording. No vague "something went wrong", no rounded-off truth about what happened.
29	- **Trustworthy:** the client never overstates what it did. Pending, failed, partial, and ambiguous outcomes are visible and distinct. Automation shows its work before it acts.
30	
31	Voice is terse and factual: short labels, plain verbs, no exclamation marks, no cheerleading.
32	
33	## Anti-references
34	
35	- **Gmail-web clutter:** toolbars of rarely-used icons, chrome competing with content, permanent competing panels.
36	- **"AI magic" email products:** AI destinations, sparkle icons, generated summaries presented as fact, fabricated contact enrichment, automation that acts without a preview.
37	- **Superhuman feature-parity clone:** Superhuman is the visual and interaction reference for browsing (layout, density, type, keyboard feel), and close look parity there is a goal. Features and workflows are our own; don't import Superhuman's product scope or claim verified behavioral parity.
38	- **Generic SaaS dashboard aesthetics:** card stacks and grids, gradient heroes, oversized rounded panels, decorative illustration or motion.
39	- **Optimistic UI that lies:** "Done" before the provider confirmed, silent retries of ambiguous sends, dead controls that look actionable.
40	
41	## Design Principles
42	
43	1. **Honest state over smooth feel.** When speed and truthfulness conflict, show the truth. Every action has a visible pending, success, partial, failed, or unknown state. Show evidence and coverage, including unknown and retained facts.
44	2. **Keyboard first, mouse welcome.** Every core triage path is reachable and discoverable from the keyboard; pointer interaction is supported, never required.
45	3. **Content is the interface.** Chrome stays quiet and compact so the list and the conversation dominate. Add UI only when it earns its space in the triage loop; reuse established commands, navigation and recovery surfaces before adding new ones.
46	4. **Preview before power.** Bulk actions, automations, and agent-proposed changes show what they will do before they do it, and report exactly what they did after. Focus, bulk selection and message identity stay separate concepts.
47	5. **Opinionated defaults, replaceable parts.** Ship one strong way of working; design surfaces so views, signals, and commands can be swapped without breaking the core experience.
48	
49	Standing constraints: ordinary reading stays local and non-mutating; message content renders as safe literal plain text; drafts stay local-only.
50	
51	## Accessibility & Inclusion
52	
53	Not a formal priority at this stage; no WCAG conformance target or certification is implied. Keyboard operability and visible focus remain required because they are core to the keyboard-first model. Don't regress behavior that already exists (explicit action labels, editable/IME shortcut protection, reduced-motion alternatives, selection/outcome announcements). The existing desktop/contact breakpoints remain authoritative; no new mobile UI. Revisit if the audience expands beyond the author.

207	# Design System: Email OS
208	
209	## 1. Overview
210	
211	**Creative North Star: "The Quiet Instrument"**
212	
213	A precision tool used in long, focused sessions. The surface is a single warm charcoal plane. The interface recedes until only the list, the open conversation and the next decision are on screen. Density is high but calm: 36px rows, small type, no dividers, no cards. One violet signal marks where you are. Everything else is a tonal step on the same warm gray ramp.
214	
215	The system follows Superhuman's browsing look closely, and that parity is an explicit goal. It covers geometry, density, type scale, tonal layering and the focused-row treatment. Features and workflows stay our own. The one place we deliberately go our own way is state: pending, failed, partial and outcome-unknown states are always visible in their own form (*"Honest state over smooth feel"*, PRODUCT.md). A quiet surface must never hide what happened.
216	
217	The system rejects Gmail-web clutter, "AI magic" sparkle chrome, generic SaaS dashboards (card grids, gradient heroes, oversized rounded panels), and optimistic UI that says "Done" before the provider confirms.
218	
219	**Key Characteristics:**
220	- Three fixed panes: a 40px icon rail, a fluid list or reader, and a 272px darker contact pane. Each is separated by a single 1px divider.
221	- One content inset (50px from the list pane's left edge). It aligns split tabs, sender names, date-group captions and banners.
222	- 36px rows on 12px type. Hierarchy comes from weight and tone, not size.
223	- Pane-edge alignment: the contact name sits on the split-tab line, and the contact email sits on the first-row line.
224	- Flat tonal layering. No shadows in the browsing shell.
225	- The violet accent appears once per screen: on the focused row or the active message.
226	
227	**Layout geometry (approximate calibration targets).** These values come from the 2026-11-07 Superhuman reference capture (1603×2000 image px). The capture was scaled by about 1.56 image px per CSS px, calibrated from the macOS traffic-light pitch of 20pt and cross-checked against the 36px rhythm and the 40px and 270px pane widths in `superhuman-email-browsing-ux-spec.md`. Verify them on real displays.
228	- **Rail:** 40px wide. The top action button (28px circle) is centered on the split-tab line (42px down). The navigation icons sit in a dark pill about 30px wide that starts near the header's bottom edge, with its first glyph centered on the first list line (96px down) and a 28px pitch. The active glyph sits on a 24px Rail Pebble disc inside the pill.
229	- **Split header:** 78px from the content top to the first row. Tabs are vertically centered about 42px down. The hamburger is centered 23px into the pane. Tabs start at the 50px content inset with an 18px gap; the count sits 4px after its label. Compose and search icons are right-aligned on the 32px action pitch.
230	- **Rows:** 36px. The highlight is inset 6px from both pane edges. There is a 44px left gutter, with the 5px unread dot centered about 34px into the row. The sender column is 132px, and subject→snippet→meta gaps are 12px. The trailing date sits about 25px from the pane edge. On focus, three 16px action glyphs replace the date at a 32px pitch.
231	- **Date groups:** a 48px block, with the caption vertically centered on the content inset.
232	- **Contact pane:** 272px with a 24px inner inset. The name is centered on the tab line (42px), the email on the first list line (96px), the "Mail" label about 36px lower (~131px) and the first thread at ~156px, then a 24px pitch. Superhuman's footer toolbar sits 24px from the bottom: a ghost label plus 16px glyphs at a 28px pitch.
233	
234	### Parity Gaps (current code → target)
235	
236	This is the backlog for layout, typeset and polish passes. Each gap names what ships today and what this spec requires.
237	
238	1. **Split header.** Done (2026-11-07 header pass). The header is one borderless 78px strip inside the list column (the rail and contact pane span its height). It has a Graphite hamburger (Destinations navigator) centered 23px in, split tabs on the 50px inset (16px, active Paper White, inactive Smoke, 11px Ash count 4px after the label, 18px apart), and right-hand glyphs on the 32px pitch: Back (when there is history), Reminders (fixture only), the Starred-only toggle, Commands and Search. There is no brand text, no visible h1 while a tab is active, and no bordered chips. Glyphs are local inline SVG (`HeaderGlyph.vue`).
239	   - The context h1 stays in the accessibility tree. It is shown on screen, styled like an active tab, only when no rendered tab is active (Cached Done, Starred, Search, the reader, an open drawer).
240	   - The status line is removed. The inbox count is on the active tab; loaded counts were dropped as duplicates of the list. Selection count stays in SelectionBar, plus a visually hidden polite announcement. The pending count is covered by row "Pending…", the action notice and Activity. The Shift+U hint is in the Commands palette. The command error is its own alert line in the in-flow notice slot beside the action notice. The read-only hint and the Unread-only/Starred-only filter states stay visible in words in the header.
241	   - The Inbox coverage sentence is the tabs' accessible description and the tab strip's hover title. The browser-preview banner is a one-line amber "Preview · in-memory" note on the right; the full disclosure is its title and accessible text.
242	   - Utility drawers now start below the header, so they never cover its glyphs.
243	   Remaining: a compose glyph was deliberately not added, because there is no compose capability beyond local drafts in the Drafts drawer; decide whether "New local draft" earns a header slot. (The aggregate pending count now lives on the Activity rail badge, and the tab line is calibrated against the rail's home circle: both are centered 42px down; see gap 2.)
244	2. **Rail.** Done (2026-11-07 rail/contact layout pass). The rail is a fixed 40px column (px, so larger root fonts widen the list, never the rail) with a 1px Seam on its right.
245	   - **Home circle:** Inbox is the 28px Rail Pebble circle, centered on the split-tab line. We have no AI or compose action to put there, so the primary destination takes the slot instead of an empty or dead control.
246	   - **Inkwell pill:** a 30px pill (the capture measures ~30px, not 28px) holds Starred (Gmail), Cached Done, Provider mail and Cached Trash (Gmail) as 16px glyphs on 28px hit targets at a 28px pitch. Its first glyph is centered on the first list line.
247	   - **Utilities:** Account (Gmail), Activity, Drafts and the narrow-viewport Contact disclosure are ghost glyphs at the bottom, 16px from the edge.
248	   - **States:** the current destination (`aria-current`) or open drawer (`aria-expanded`) shows a Paper White glyph on a 24px Rail Pebble disc; the rest are Graphite and rise to Paper White on hover and focus.
249	   - **Labels:** every button keeps its text label as its accessible name (a visually hidden span, so `textContent` is unchanged), its hover `title` (the action label with its shortcut, as on the header glyphs), and a keyboard tooltip: the same label shown beside the rail on `:focus-visible`, with Popover lift.
250	   - **Activity badge:** a small Amber Notice count on the Activity glyph shows unresolved operations, i.e. `queued`/`applying` plus `outcome_unknown`. It is derived from the activity rows the drawer already lists, with no new read.
